segments.text: Marketing is the process of understanding customer needs, creating and delivering value that satisfies those needs, and building lasting exchange relationships that support the organization’s goals — it is deliberately broader than “selling,” which is only one narrow activity (persuading someone to buy something already produced) within this much wider process. This unit follows the marketing process roughly in sequence: understand the environment and the customer, segment the market and choose targets, gather information to support decisions, then design the actual offering (branding, product life-cycle management, pricing, distribution, and communication).
Three foundational terms must be distinguished precisely, since exam questions regularly test the difference:

items.text: is a basic state of felt deprivation — hunger, the need for shelter, the need for esteem — these are not created by marketing; they are basic human states.
is the specific form a need takes as it is shaped by culture and individual personality — hunger (a need) might take the want-form of a specific cuisine or brand of food.
is a want backed by both the ability and the willingness to pay for it — many people may want a luxury car, but only those able and willing to actually purchase one represent demand for it.

segments.text: is the comparison a customer makes between the perceived benefits of an offering and its perceived costs (not only its price, but also time, effort, and psychological costs of obtaining it) — an organization creates value by increasing perceived benefits, decreasing perceived costs, or both. Marketing begins before a sale, with understanding these needs, and continues after a sale through delivery, customer satisfaction, and relationship-building — reinforcing that marketing is a continuous process, not a single transactional event.

Marketing environmental scanning studies the same broad forces introduced in the Management unit’s discussion of the organizational environment, applied specifically to marketing decisions. It is useful to distinguish:

items.text: — actors close to the firm that directly affect its ability to serve customers: the company itself, suppliers, marketing intermediaries (resellers, logistics firms), competitors, various publics (media, government, financial community), and customers.

— the broader demographic, economic, technological, political/legal, social/cultural, and natural forces shaping the whole market (the same PESTEL-style categories introduced earlier, applied here to identify marketing-relevant opportunities and threats specifically).

segments.text: Consumer analysis studies how individuals and households move through the process of recognizing a need, searching for information, evaluating alternatives, making a purchase, and responding afterward. A simple five-stage consumer decision process is:

items.text: — the consumer perceives a difference between an actual and a desired state.
— gathering information from personal sources (family, friends), commercial sources (advertising, salespeople), public sources (media, reviews), and experiential sources (trying the product).
— comparing options against criteria the consumer considers important.
— selecting and buying a specific option (which can still be disrupted at the last stage by others’ attitudes or unexpected situational factors).
— the consumer’s satisfaction or dissatisfaction, and resulting likelihood of repeat purchase or negative word-of-mouth.

The product life-cycle (PLC) concept describes a common (though not universal) pattern products follow across four stages:

items.text: — the product is new to the market; sales are low, promotional costs are high (building awareness), and profits are often negative or minimal.
— sales rise rapidly as the market becomes aware of the product and adopts it; competitors typically begin to enter, attracted by the visible growth.
— sales growth slows and eventually plateaus as the market becomes saturated; competition is intense, and the emphasis shifts toward differentiation and cost efficiency to defend market share.

— sales fall, often due to changing customer preferences or new technology; firms must decide whether to harvest the product (minimize investment and maximize remaining cash flow), reposition it for a new use or market, or withdraw it entirely.

segments.text: An important caution the syllabus explicitly flags: the PLC is a useful descriptive model of a common pattern, not a strict law that every product follows in exactly this order or timing — some products skip stages, some cycle back into renewed growth after apparent maturity (through reformulation or repositioning), and the length of each stage varies enormously by product and industry.

Pricing decisions must simultaneously consider customer-perceived value, the organization’s own costs, competitive prices, and broader strategic objectives — pricing cannot be decided from cost alone, because a price set without reference to customer value or the competitive landscape can be entirely wrong even if it is calculated with perfect cost accuracy. Three broad pricing approaches:

items.text: starts from the cost of producing the offering and adds a target margin.

starts from the customer’s perceived value of the offering, and works backward to a price the customer would consider fair for that perceived value — potentially allowing a higher price than cost-based methods would produce, if perceived value is genuinely high.

sets price with primary reference to competitors’ prices and the customer’s expectations formed by the broader market, rather than starting from either the firm’s own costs or its own assessment of customer value.

segments.text: Pricing decisions affect far more than immediate revenue: they shape demand levels, signal and reinforce (or undermine) the intended brand position, and affect relationships with distribution-channel partners (who typically expect their own margin built into the final price) — a reminder that pricing, like every element of the marketing mix, must be coordinated with the other elements rather than decided in isolation.

Integrated Marketing Communications is the coordinated use of multiple communication tools — advertising, sales promotion, public relations, personal selling, and direct/digital communication — so that customers receive a clear, consistent message about the brand across every channel through which they encounter it. The critical, frequently-tested nuance here is that
consistency does not require every message to be identical

; it requires that different messages, tailored to different channels and audiences, all reinforce the same underlying brand position and customer value proposition, rather than sending contradictory signals about what the brand actually stands for. A well-executed IMC campaign might use different messages, tone, and format on social media, through in-store sales staff, and via public relations — while ensuring all three consistently support the same core value proposition.
Key takeaways for the Marketing unit

items.text: Marketing is deliberately broader than selling: it begins with understanding needs before a product even exists, and continues after the sale through satisfaction and relationship management.

The segmentation-targeting-positioning (STP) sequence is fixed and must not be confused: segmentation divides the market, targeting selects among the resulting segments, and positioning shapes how the chosen segment perceives the offer.
The marketing mix (4 Ps, extended to 7 Ps for services) is the tactical toolkit through which marketing strategy — the choice of target customers and value proposition — is actually implemented.

Pricing, like every mix element, must be coordinated with the others: a price set from cost alone, ignoring customer value and competitors, is incomplete regardless of how accurately the cost component itself was calculated.
